title: Subcube partition complexity versus query complexity
formal: Determine the optimal universal exponent function \(\alpha:\{\mathrm{det},\mathrm{rand}\}\to\mathbb R\) defined by \[\alpha(m)=\inf\{a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:\ \exists C>0\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall\text{ nonconstant }f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\},\ M_m(f)\le C\,\mathrm{UC}(f)^a\},\] where \(M_{\mathrm{det}}=D\) and \(M_{\mathrm{rand}}=R_{1/3}\) are the query measures below. The constant \(C\) may depend on \(m,a\), but not on \(n,f\).
why: Subcube partitions give globally consistent certificates without requiring an algorithm to discover them through successive probes. The largest gap measures the limitations of this certificate-based view of classical query complexity, including several important lower-bound methods.
status_note: Resolved at the optimal classical exponent level by Ambainis, Kokainis and Kothari, CCC 2016, Theorems 1.2–1.3 and 5.1: both specified exponents equal 2. The relevant proof chain and model transfer were checked on 2026-09-16, including the supporting framework’s 2019 revision. This does not claim a Lean-verified proof, exact constants, or resolution of a quantum or iterated-majority variant.

importance.reason: An influential comparison between adaptive computation and unambiguous certificates for total Boolean functions, with consequences for the strength of classical query lower bounds. This is an assessment of the historical question’s significance, not a reason to retain a resolved target in the active benchmark.

sentences: A subcube partition covers all Boolean inputs by disjoint monochromatic sets, each described by fixing some coordinates.
Its complexity is the maximum number of fixed coordinates needed by a part.
A decision tree must discover an answer through successive input queries, and may be deterministic or have bounded random error.
The historical question asks how large a polynomial gap can occur between these classical query costs and partition complexity.
Nearly quadratic separations published in 2016 match the universal quadratic upper bound at the exponent level, so this card is retained as a resolved archival record.

definitions:
A subcube of \(\{0,1\}^n\) is the nonempty set of strings satisfying a partial assignment \(x_j=b_j\) on a subset \(S\subseteq[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(b_j\in\{0,1\}\). Its width is \(|S|\). A monochromatic subcube partition for \(f\) is a finite collection of pairwise disjoint subcubes whose union is \(\{0,1\}^n\), such that \(f\) is constant on each subcube. Its cost is the largest width of a part, and \(\mathrm{UC}(f)\) is the minimum cost over all such partitions. No sequential tree structure is required of the partition. The measure counts fixed coordinates, not the number of parts.

A deterministic decision tree has an input-coordinate label \(j\in[n]\) at each internal node, two outgoing edges labeled \(0,1\), and a Boolean output at each leaf. On input \(x\), it follows the edge labeled \(x_j\) whenever it queries coordinate \(j\). Its query cost is its maximum root-to-leaf depth. Let \(D(f)\) be the minimum cost of a finite tree returning \(f(x)\) for every input \(x\). A randomized decision tree of cost at most \(t\) is a probability distribution on finite deterministic trees of depth at most the integer \(t\). It succeeds when, for every fixed input \(x\), the probability of returning \(f(x)\) is at least \(2/3\). Define \(R_{1/3}(f)\) to be the minimum such \(t\). The distribution is independent of \(x\); cost is worst-case over inputs and trees in its support, rather than expected query count.

For each fixed \(n,f\), the tree, distribution and partition may depend arbitrarily on the entire function \(f\). These are query measures: only probes to the unknown input \(x\) are charged; local computation and the description of \(f\) have no cost restriction. There is no uniform algorithm that must receive a representation of \(f\), no promise restricting \(x\), and no quantum queries. Nonconstant functions ensure \(\mathrm{UC}(f)\ge1\). The known universal inequality \(R_{1/3}(f)\le D(f)\le\mathrm{UC}(f)^2\) makes the defining set nonempty and both exponents finite. The infimum definition does not require attainment at its endpoint.
answer_criterion: The historical benchmark requires a supplied function \(g:\{\mathrm{det},\mathrm{rand}\}\to\mathbb R\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that \(|g(m)-\alpha(m)|\le1/100\) for both domain elements. A one-sided estimate alone is insufficient; a certified interval of width at most \(1/50\) for each value qualifies via its midpoint. The accepted precision concerns these real exponents, not exact multiplicative constants or lower-order logarithmic factors. This archived record has the known answer \(\alpha(\mathrm{det})=\alpha(\mathrm{rand})=2\); the editorial proof review is not itself a Lean formalization.

context_blocks.text: The 2015 conclusion asks for the strongest separation between subcube partition complexity and query complexity, expressly including deterministic queries. This record interprets strongest asymptotic separation by the optimal polynomial exponent, for the deterministic and bounded-error randomized classical branches. It does not replace that question with the separate exact complexity of the iterated majority function mentioned alongside it.

Ambainis, Kokainis and Kothari prove nearly quadratic lower separations for both measures in CCC 2016, matching the universal quadratic upper bound at the exponent level. Thus both values of the function specified here are \(2\).

This exponent-level resolution does not assert matching absolute constants or remove every lower-order factor. Quantum query complexity is a separate comparison and is not part of this card’s domain. The full historical record and original source passage are retained in the archive.

checked_sources: Read the original APPROX/RANDOM 2015 Section 2 models and Section 5 open-question paragraph on printed page 929. The adjacent precise 4-MAJ and expected partition-bound questions are distinct and are not claimed resolved.

Read CCC 2016 Sections 1 and 3–5 through the complete classical proof of Theorem 5.1. Matched UC=max(UC0,UC1) with monochromatic subcube partition maximum codimension, and R with per-input bounded error and worst-case queries.

Checked universal upper bound D<=C0*C1<=UC^2: iterated consistent 0-certificates cost at most C0 per phase and reduce the residual 1-certificate bound by at least one unless the function is decided. R<=D then gives exponent upper bound 2.

Checked the fixed-k induction: input length N_k=O(n^(25^k)), R(f_k)=soft-Omega(n^(2k+1)), and UC(f_k)=soft-O(n^(k+1)); constants and polylog exponents may depend on fixed k. For any a<2 choose fixed k with (2k+1)/(k+1)>a; letting n grow defeats every universal C. This proves the infimum equals 2 without needing uniformity in k or an exact quadratic witness.

Read supporting Aaronson–Ben-David–Kothari arXiv:1511.01937v2 Lemma 6 pages 12–13 and Lemma 21 pages 23–24. Checked the blank-cell, address-hybrid argument and deterministic adversary transfer. Corrected sign/constant slips in the displayed randomized balancing explanation during audit: an event gap delta can be balanced to worst-case distinguishing advantage at least delta/4, sufficient for the claimed Omega(R/log^2 N) bound. No exact displayed 1/(12c) constant is needed.

Read Goos–Jayram–Pitassi–Watson ECCC15/169 Lemma 6 and complete Section 5.1 proof: plant an input in a uniform block, sample other blocks from the 1-input distribution, truncate at 8q/k, and apply minimax. This verifies worst-case randomized AND composition; OR follows by complementing f and the output.

Checked harmless presentation slips in CCC Lemma 3.1/Section 5: an AND 0-certificate uses the first 0-block and preceding 1-blocks; the sum of two upper-bound terms can be replaced by twice their maximum in the asymptotic estimate. These do not change the exponent result.
